title: Protein distances: when counting isn't enough

prompts.concept: These are protein sequences evolved under the JTT model, but the matrix on screen is the plain p-distance: the fraction of sites that differ. Which two taxa join first?
prompts.math: NJ joins the pair minimizing Q(i,j) = (n−2)·d(i,j) − R_i − R_j, where d is the observed fraction of differing sites. Use the Distance/Q switch to see Q directly — the smallest off-diagonal value wins.
prompts.reveal: C and D join first — they are genuinely closest. Now click the C–F cell to open "How was this distance computed?": the count says 0.42, but JTT's likelihood estimate is 0.61. F evolved three times faster than its neighbours, so many of its sites were substituted more than once and the count never saw them.

prompts.concept: Four clusters remain: E, the (C,D) pair, the (A,B) pair and the (F,G) pair. On the true tree E sits next to (F,G) — but F raced ahead on its long branch, and the raw counts make that neighbourhood look no closer than the others.
prompts.math: A branch of 0.30 accumulates about 30 changes per 100 sites, but two changes can hit the same site — the second erases the first from the count. Long branches always look shorter under p.

prompts.concept: The tree is complete, but RF = 2: counting differences pulled E toward the (A,B) group instead of (F,G). Every underestimate was largest along F's fast lineage, which reshaped the join order. Switch the Correction control to JTT — it scores each observed difference against how likely that amino-acid exchange is — and the same sequences recover the true tree (RF = 0).
prompts.math: JTT finds the branch length d that maximizes log L(d) = Σ N_xy ln(π_x P_xy(d)): pairs that differ often between frequently exchanged amino acids score less distance than the same count between rare-exchange pairs. Click any cell to see this fit for a pair.
